module Spam
  # This module is responsible for handling spam in our various user input sources.
  #
  # @note We may not immediately block spam but instead slowly escalate our response.
  module Handler
    # These are purely words that can help trigger an investigation.
    # They are never to be used to directly take any action.
    # They can absolutely be used out of context and only exist to trigger investigation.
    # Depending on the forem, they are hypothetically not even abuse in any way.
    PROFILE_SPAM_TRIGGER_TERMS = [
      "buy links",
      "buying links",
      "backlinks",
      "link building",
      "seo services",
      "casino",
      "gambling",
      "betting",
      "escort",
      "prostitut",
      "adult",
      "girls",
      "porn",
      "onlyfans",
      "crypto pump",
      "forex signals",
      "loan shark",
    ].freeze
    # @return [TrueClass] if we are going to try to use more rigorous spam handling
    # @return [FalseClass] if we are using less rigorous spam handling
    def self.more_rigorous_user_profile_spam_checking?
      FeatureFlag.enabled?(:more_rigorous_user_profile_spam_checking)
    end

    # @return [TrueClass] if we are going to unpublish articles when we auto-suspend
    # @return [FalseClass] if we are not going to unpublish articles when we auto-suspend
    def self.unpublish_all_posts_when_user_auto_suspended?
      FeatureFlag.enabled?(:unpublish_all_posts_when_user_auto_suspended)
    end

    # Test the article for spamminess.  If it's not spammy, don't do anything.
    #
    # If it is spammy, escalate the situation!
    #
    # @param article [Article] the article to check for spamminess
    # @param attributes [Array<Symbol>] test these attributes of the article.
    def self.handle_article!(article:, attributes: %i[title body_markdown])
      if article_linked_domain_spam?(article)
        article.update_column(:automod_label, "clear_and_obvious_spam")
        article.automod_label = "clear_and_obvious_spam"
      else
        # First, run content moderation labeling
        label_article_content!(article)
      end

      # Handle clear and obvious violations immediately
      if %w[clear_and_obvious_spam clear_and_obvious_harmful clear_and_obvious_inciting].include?(article.automod_label)
        issue_spam_reaction_for!(reactable: article)

        if Reaction.user_has_been_given_too_many_spammy_article_reactions?(
          user: article.user,
          include_user_profile: more_rigorous_user_profile_spam_checking?,
        )
          suspend!(user: article.user)
        end

        return :spam
      end

      # High quality content bypasses spam checks entirely
      if %w[very_good_and_on_topic great_and_on_topic very_good_but_offtopic_for_subforem
            great_but_off_topic_for_subforem].include?(article.automod_label)
        return :not_spam
      end

      # For likely violations, bypass badge count and other restrictions but still run checks
      bypass_restrictions = %w[likely_spam likely_harmful likely_inciting].include?(article.automod_label)

      # Continue with existing spam detection logic
      text = attributes.map { |attr| article.public_send(attr) }.join("\n")

      # Check if we should trigger spam detection
      should_check = Settings::RateLimit.trigger_spam_for?(text: text) ||
        (article.processed_html.include?("<a") && Ai::Base::DEFAULT_KEY.present? &&
         (bypass_restrictions || article.user.badge_achievements_count < 4) &&
         Ai::ArticleCheck.new(article).spam?)

      return :not_spam unless should_check

      issue_spam_reaction_for!(reactable: article)

      return unless Reaction.user_has_been_given_too_many_spammy_article_reactions?(
        user: article.user,
        include_user_profile: more_rigorous_user_profile_spam_checking?,
      )

      suspend!(user: article.user)
    end

    # Test the comment for spamminess.  If it's not spammy, don't do anything.
    #
    # If it is spammy, escalate the situation!
    #
    # @param comment [Comment] the comment to check for spamminess
    def self.handle_comment!(comment:)
      # Existing checks for trusted users.
      return :not_spam if comment.user.badge_achievements_count > 6
      return :not_spam if comment.user.base_subscriber?

      if (domain = extract_first_domain_from(comment.processed_html)) && extensive_domain_spam?(domain: domain,
                                                                                                current_comment: comment)
        issue_spam_reaction_for!(reactable: comment)
        suspend_if_user_is_repeat_offender(user: comment.user)
        return :spam # Return early as it's confirmed spam.
      end

      rate_limit_spam = Settings::RateLimit.trigger_spam_for?(text: comment.body_markdown)

      # Return if neither of the spam conditions are met.
      return :not_spam unless rate_limit_spam ||
        (comment.processed_html.include?("<a") && Ai::Base::DEFAULT_KEY.present? && Ai::CommentCheck.new(comment).spam?)

      issue_spam_reaction_for!(reactable: comment)
      suspend_if_user_is_repeat_offender(user: comment.user)
    end

    # Test the user for spamminess.  If it's not spammy, don't do anything.
    #
    # If it is spammy, escalate the situation!
    #
    # @param user [User] the user to check for spamminess
    def self.handle_user!(user:)
      text = [user.name]

      if more_rigorous_user_profile_spam_checking?
        text += [
          user.email,
          user.github_username,
          user.profile&.website_url,
          user.profile&.location,
          user.profile&.summary,
          user.twitter_username,
          user.username,
        ].compact
      end

      text = text.join("\n")

      return :not_spam unless Settings::RateLimit.trigger_spam_for?(text: text)

      issue_spam_reaction_for!(reactable: user)
    end

    # Test a user profile update for clear and obvious spam or abuse.
    #

module FasttextClassification

  # Fasttext params 

  EPOCH = 50
  LR = 1.0
  WS = 8
  WORD_NGRAMS = 4
  MIN_COUNT = 3

  # Training text config

  MIN_LINK_WORD_SIZE = 2

  MODEL_PATH = "trove/fasttext-model.ftz"

  # Reporting config

  MIN_SCORE_TO_TEST = 0.999
  SAVE_NUMBER = 49

  def self.train(lq_score: 1, hq_score: 136, save: true)
    p "Training with lq limit of #{lq_score} and hq limit of #{hq_score}, and a save setting of #{save}."
    required_columns = "id, title, cached_tag_list, body_markdown, html"
    low_quality_set = Entity.select(required_columns).where("current_appropriateness_score < #{lq_score}").order("created_at DESC").limit(26500).partition { rand(10) != 0 }
    high_quality_set = Entity.select(required_columns).where("current_appropriateness_score > #{hq_score}").order("created_at DESC").limit(26500).partition { rand(10) != 0 }
    p "Fetched data, let's go!"
    classifier = FastText::Classifier.new(epoch: EPOCH, lr: LR, ws: WS, word_ngrams: WORD_NGRAMS, min_count: MIN_COUNT)
    fasttext_train(classifier, low_quality_set.first , high_quality_set.first)
    num = final_test(classifier, low_quality_set.second, high_quality_set.second)
    if save && num > SAVE_NUMBER
      p "Saving... with number of #{num}"
      classifier.quantize unless Rails.env.test?
      classifier.save_model(MODEL_PATH) unless Rails.env.test?  
    end
  end

  def self.classify(entity, force = false)
    return { "confidence" => 0.99, "label" => "high_quality"} if (Rails.env.test? && force == false) || !File.exist?(MODEL_PATH)

    result = FastText.load_model(MODEL_PATH).predict(trainable_text(entity))
    {
      "confidence" => result.values.first,
      "label" => result.keys.first
    }
  end

    low_range.each do |n|
      3.times do
        self.train(lq_score: n, save: false)
      end
    end
    high_range.each do |n|
      3.times do
        self.train(hq_score: n, save: false)
      end
    end
  end

    text = []

    hq_set.each do |entity|

      labels << "high_quality"
    end
    classifier.fit(text, labels)

    entities = Entity.published_articles.where("created_at > ?", 25.hour.ago).order("RANDOM()").where("current_appropriateness_score > 99").limit(24)
    return if entities.size < 10 # We only want to take action if there is at least a few available entities.
    
    response = Ai.top_quality_entity_from_group(entities)
    return unless response[:result] == "success"

    entity = Entity.find_by(path: URI.parse(response[:output]).path)
    # Create action under "first user" for initial testing
    LabelAction.create(user_id: User.first.id, entity_id: entity.id, label: "good_content") if entity
  end

  def detect_most_likely_spam_from_group
    # Periodically use AI to determine which recent entity is most likely to be the highest quality.
    # Accuracy of this pick is enforced by selecting from a large number of entities which are already in the category of human-determined likely spam
    # and only taking action on the most likely spam *relative* to others.
    entities = Entity.published_articles.order("RANDOM()").where("current_appropriateness_score > 0 AND current_appropriateness_score < 22").limit(24)
    return if entities.size < 15 # We only want to take action if there is a backlog of spam to process.

    response = Ai.spam_entity_from_group(entities)
    return unless response[:result] == "success"

    entity = Entity.find_by(path: URI.parse(response[:output]).path)
    # Create action under "first user" for initial testing
    LabelAction.create(user_id: User.first.id, entity_id: entity.id, label: "spam") if entity
  end

  def detect_egregious_generic_automation_from_group
    # Periodically use AI to determine which recent entity is most likely to be the highest quality.
    # Accuracy of this pick is enforced by selecting from a large number of entities which are already in the category of human-determined likely spam
    # and only taking action on the most likely spam *relative* to others.

module FasttextClassification

  EPOCH = 50

  WS = 8

  # Training text config

  # Reporting config

  SAVE_NUMBER = 49

  def self.train(lq_score: 1, hq_score: 136, save: true)
    p "Training with lq limit of #{lq_score} and hq limit of #{hq_score}, and a save setting of #{save}."
    required_columns = "id, title, cached_tag_list, body_markdown, html"
    low_quality_set = Entity.select(required_columns).where("current_appropriateness_score < #{lq_score}").order("created_at DESC").limit(26500).partition { rand(10) != 0 }
    high_quality_set = Entity.select(required_columns).where("current_appropriateness_score > #{hq_score}").order("created_at DESC").limit(26500).partition { rand(10) != 0 }
    p "Fetched data, let's go!"
    classifier = FastText::Classifier.new(epoch: EPOCH, lr: LR, ws: WS, word_ngrams: WORD_NGRAMS, min_count: MIN_COUNT)
    fasttext_train(classifier, low_quality_set.first , high_quality_set.first)
    num = final_test(classifier, low_quality_set.second, high_quality_set.second)
    if save && num > SAVE_NUMBER
      p "Saving... with number of #{num}"
      classifier.quantize unless Rails.env.test?
      classifier.save_model(MODEL_PATH) unless Rails.env.test?  
    end
  end

  def self.classify(entity, force = false)
    return { "confidence" => 0.99, "label" => "high_quality"} if (Rails.env.test? && force == false) || !File.exist?(MODEL_PATH)

    result = FastText.load_model(MODEL_PATH).predict(trainable_text(entity))
    {
      "confidence" => result.values.first,
      "label" => result.keys.first
    }
  end

  def self.train_ranges_experimentally(low_range, high_range)
    low_range.each do |n|
      3.times do
        self.train(lq_score: n, save: false)
      end
    end
    high_range.each do |n|
      3.times do
        self.train(hq_score: n, save: false)
      end
    end
  end

  private

  def self.fasttext_train(classifier, lq_set, hq_set)
    text = []
    labels = []
    p "Training on low quality set of #{lq_set.size} records"
    lq_set.each do |entity|
      text << trainable_text(entity)
      labels << "low_quality"
    end

    p "Training on high quality set of #{hq_set.size} records"
    hq_set.each do |entity|
      text << trainable_text(entity)
      labels << "high_quality"
    end
    classifier.fit(text, labels)
  end

  def self.classification_test(classifier, dataset)

# TypeSafe Jev Model Summary

**Model Name/Version:**
- `jev-1.13.0` (current)
- Aliases: `jev-latest` and `jev-preview` (both point to 1.13.0)

**Context Window:**
64k tokens per request; 32k for `state` plus the longest question combined.

**Pricing:**
"$42 / $0.042" per billion/million input tokens respectively. Output tokens incur no charge.

**Latency:**
Not specified in the documentation.

**Language Support:**
"English is the primary training language and where accuracy is currently best." Other languages including CJK scripts are supported but with lower accuracy; testing recommended before production use.

**Content Moderation/Security Notes:**
- Text-only input; non-text (images, audio, video) must be preprocessed into text
- "Jev is not trained on customer requests or responses"
- Enterprise customers can access zero data retention options
- No fine-tuning with customer data; customization occurs through request parameters (`state`, `instructions`, `criteria`)

**Rate Limits:**
250,000 tokens/second and 1,200 requests/minute, though the documentation notes these "can change without notice" during high demand periods.

content.text:
Jev would work best as a cheap, calibrated second opinion next to Gemini, not as a replacement. Gemini's spam checks answer only YES or NO, so today we can't set thresholds, can't tell a confident call from a guess, and can't measure how accurate they are. Jev returns calibrated probabilities (a 0.9 is right about 9 times in 10), costs $0.042 per million input tokens with free output, and takes about 600ms, similar to our Gemini calls. I read everything from `origin/main` and didn't switch branches, because your working tree has uncommitted changes.

**Current spam checks on Forem main (last 24h in prod):**

| Service | Calls/day | Avg input tokens | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Ai::ContentModerationLabeler` | 5,417 | 2,050 | Picks 1 of 15 labels plus a compellingness score (JSON) |
| `Ai::ArticleCheck` | 1,835 | 2,521 | YES/NO; only runs on posts with links from authors with fewer than 4 badges |
| `Ai::ProfileModerationLabeler` | 400 | 957 | Picks a label for the user profile |
| `Ai::CommentCheck` | 365 | 1,479 | YES/NO; only runs on comments that contain a link |

Running Jev on all of these would be about 20M tokens a day, which is under $1. On Gemini errors, `ArticleCheck` and `CommentCheck` quietly return `false` (not spam), so any outage lets spam straight through.

## Where Jev fits

1. **Shadow mode first.** Add an `Ai::Jev` client that mirrors `Ai::Base`: HTTParty, `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone`, gated on a `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` env var, and logging to `AiAudit` so we get the audit trail for free. Wherever `Spam::Handler` calls Gemini, also ask Jev one yes/no question ("is this spam?") and record the probability, without changing any behavior. After a couple of weeks, compare the scores against real moderator outcomes (mod vomit reactions, the `spam` role, suspensions) to choose thresholds from data rather than guesses.
2. **Tiered checks in `Spam::Handler`.** Once thresholds exist, run Jev on everything, since it's cheap enough to drop the link-only and badge-count restrictions:
   - Probability above ~0.97: act straight away.
   - Probability below ~0.05: skip `ArticleCheck`/`CommentCheck`.
   - Anything in between: fall through to the Gemini check we already have.

   This covers more content, including comment spam with no links (phone numbers, "crypto recovery" scams), and cuts Gemini calls.
3. **Both models must agree before suspending.** `suspend!` is the high-cost false positive. Require Jev and Gemini to both say spam before an automatic suspension; either one alone still gives a spam reaction.
4. **Keep `ContentModerationLabeler` on Gemini for now.** Its labels and compellingness score feed feed ranking and subforem reassignment. Jev's pick-one question type could replicate the 15 labels, but that touches feed sorting. Revisit once the shadow data looks good.

## forem-tools (Shield)

- **Replace or supplement FastText.** `FasttextClassification` is a self-trained model that has to be retrained and drifts over time. Jev needs no training data (the published benchmark shows F1 0.952 without training, versus trained classifiers that break when the domain shifts). Its probability could be one more term in `Entity#calculate_appropriateness`.
- **`QualityAutomationJob`.** It asks Gemini to pick the single most-spammy post out of 24, then labels it. Jev could score all 24 and label every post above a threshold.
- **`Ai.determine_resolvability`** (abuse reports). This already has three outcomes (`confirmed_abuse`, `determined_invalid`, `unclear`), which maps directly onto Jev's pick-one question. We'd get a probability per outcome and could auto-resolve only when confident.

## Caveats

- English is Jev's strongest language, and DEV gets a lot of non-English gambling and betting spam. Check accuracy on that slice during shadow mode.
- Input is capped at 32k tokens for the content plus the question, so long post bodies need truncating the way the labeler already does.
- Rate limits are 1,200 requests per minute, far above our volume.

Suggested first PR: the `Ai::Jev` client plus shadow logging in `Spam::Handler`, on a new branch off `main`. Want me to build it?

Sources:
- [TypeSafe API reference](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md)
- [TypeSafe models, pricing and limits](https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md)
- [Freek Van der Herten: Detecting spam with Jev](https://freek.dev/3194-detecting-spam-and-auto-replies-with-jev-and-the-laravel-ai-sdk)
- [pniessen/jev-test benchmark](https://github.com/pniessen/jev-test)

module Articles
  class HandleSpamWorker
    include Sidekiq::Job

    sidekiq_options queue: :high_priority

    def perform(article_id)
      article = Article.find_by(id: article_id)
      return unless article

      # Always run spam handling and score update
      Spam::Handler.handle_article!(article: article)
      article.reload.update_score

      # Only enhance if clickbait score is 0 (not already processed) and score is >= 0 (good quality after spam check)
      return unless article.clickbait_score.zero? && article.score >= 0

      enhance_article(article)
    end

    private

    def enhance_article(article)
      # Create AI client for dependency injection
      ai_client = Ai::Base.new
      enhancer = Ai::ArticleEnhancer.new(article, ai_client: ai_client)

      # Calculate and update clickbait score
      clickbait_score = enhancer.calculate_clickbait_score
      article.update_column(:clickbait_score, clickbait_score)

      # Generate and apply tags if article has no tags and meets criteria
      if should_generate_tags?(article, clickbait_score)
        suggested_tags = enhancer.generate_tags
        apply_tags_to_article(article, suggested_tags) if suggested_tags.any?
      end
    rescue StandardError => e
      Rails.logger.error("Article enhancement failed for article #{article.id}: #{e}")
    end

    def should_generate_tags?(article, clickbait_score)
      article.cached_tag_list.blank? &&
        article.score >= 0 &&
        clickbait_score < 0.6
    end

    def apply_tags_to_article(article, tag_names)
      # Validate that all suggested tags exist and are supported
      valid_tags = Tag.supported.where(name: tag_names).pluck(:name)

      if valid_tags.any?
        # Apply tags to article
        article.tag_list = valid_tags
        article.cached_tag_list = valid_tags.join(", ")
        article.save

        Rails.logger.info("Applied tags #{valid_tags.join(', ')} to article #{article.id}")
      else
        Rails.logger.warn("No valid tags found from suggestions #{tag_names.join(', ')} for article #{article.id}")
      end
    end
  end
end

module Articles
  class LabelCleanupWorker
    include Sidekiq::Job

    sidekiq_options queue: :high_priority

    # Maximum number of articles to process per run
    MAX_ARTICLES_PER_RUN = 150

    def perform
      # Find and select articles published in the last 48 hours but not in the last 10 minutes
      # that have the automod_label of "no_moderation_label"
      selected_articles = find_eligible_articles

      if selected_articles.any?
        Rails.logger.info("LabelCleanupWorker: Processing #{selected_articles.size} articles with no_moderation_label")

        # Process each selected article
        selected_articles.each do |article|
          Articles::HandleSpamWorker.perform_async(article.id)
        end

        Rails.logger.info("LabelCleanupWorker: Enqueued #{selected_articles.size} HandleSpamWorker jobs")
      else
        Rails.logger.info("LabelCleanupWorker: No eligible articles found for processing")
      end
    end

    private

    def find_eligible_articles
      # Articles published in the last 48 hours but not in the last 10 minutes
      # that have automod_label of "no_moderation_label"
      # Using >= for 48.hours.ago (inclusive) and < for 10.minutes.ago (exclusive)
      forty_eight_hours_ago = 48.hours.ago
      ten_minutes_ago = 10.minutes.ago
      
      # Add a small buffer to handle precision issues
      forty_eight_hours_ago = forty_eight_hours_ago - 1.second
      
      Article.published
             .where(automod_label: "no_moderation_label")
             .where("score > -80")
             .where("published_at >= ? AND published_at < ?", forty_eight_hours_ago, ten_minutes_ago)
             .order(published_at: :asc)
             .limit(MAX_ARTICLES_PER_RUN)
    end
  end
end

---
name: forem-after-commit-saved-changes-trap
description: "On Forem's Comment (and similar models) saved_changes is unreliable inside after_commit, because after_save hooks touch the record"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 685bb3b8-3aa7-495a-9672-781f1c07fdfc
  modified: 2026-08-16T13:27:06.949Z
---

In Forem, `after_commit` callbacks on `Comment` (and any model whose `after_save`
hooks touch the record) cannot trust `saved_changes` / `previous_changes`.
`Comment#expire_root_fragment` calls `touch` on self from an `after_save` hook;
`touch` runs `changes_applied`, so by commit time the dirty state has collapsed
to `["updated_at"]` and every real edit looks like a no-op.

**Why:** it silently makes `if: proc { saved_changes.include?("...") }` guards
dead rather than erroring, so the callback just never fires.

**How to apply:** snapshot the keys in an `after_save` (which `touch` does not
fire) and clear the snapshot in an `after_commit` registered *after* the reader,
or the snapshot outlives its save — a later bare touch on the same instance
(e.g. a comment touching its article's `last_comment_at`) will replay it. See
`ActivityTrackable#trackable_changed_keys`, added in forem#23736.

**Suspected latent bug, not fixed:** `app/models/comment.rb:96`
`after_update_commit :update_notifications, if: proc { |c| c.saved_changes.include? "body_markdown" }`
appears dead for exactly this reason — worth confirming before relying on
comment-edit notifications.

Also note `Article#title` and `Article#published` are re-derived from the
body_markdown front matter on every save, so assigning them directly in specs
or scripts is silently reverted; edit the markdown instead.

    user.touch(:last_comment_at) if user&.persisted?

    # return if nothing has changed in body markdown
    return unless saved_change_to_body_markdown? || created_at > 1.minute.ago

    Comments::HandleSpamWorker.perform_async(id)
  end

    Comments::SendEmailNotificationWorker.perform_in(120.seconds, id)

content.text:
They haven't been checked yet. All three were posted 2–5 minutes before I looked, and none of them has any Gemini call logged. This isn't a one-off: on Forem `main`, most new articles skip the immediate spam check.

**The cause.** `Article` queues the spam check from an `after_save` callback (`app/models/article.rb:350` → `create_conditional_autovomits`), and that callback runs *inside* the save transaction. Sidekiq often picks the job up before the transaction commits. When it does, `Articles::HandleSpamWorker` can't find the article yet, gets `nil` back, and returns without logging anything.

Timing from publish to the Gemini label, for articles published in the last 3 hours:

| How the article was published | Labeled within 30s | Labeled by the cleanup job (10–40 min) |
|---|---|---|
| Published straight away when created | 39 | 304 |
| Saved as a draft, published later (row already committed) | 69 | 1 |

The three articles you linked were all published straight away when created. They'll only be checked when `Articles::LabelCleanupWorker` runs at :05 and :35 past the hour, and it only picks up articles more than 10 minutes old. These three should go through at 21:05 UTC. The average delay is about 18 minutes and the longest was 40, and new spam sits unlabeled on the site for that whole time. The cleanup job also skips articles with a score of -80 or below.

Comments don't seem to have this problem: 27 of 29 recent comments with links were checked right away.

**Fix.** Keep the conditions in `after_save`, where the "what changed" checks are still reliable, but delay the enqueue until the transaction commits:

```ruby
# app/models/article.rb
Articles::HandleSpamWorker.perform_async(id)
# becomes
ActiveRecord.after_all_transactions_commit { Articles::HandleSpamWorker.perform_async(id) }
```

I'd avoid switching to `after_commit`: another `after_save` callback on the model can reset what the record thinks changed before commit time, and the change conditions would quietly stop working.

The car-fridge article may still get through after it's checked. It has no links, so the Gemini `ArticleCheck` never runs on it, and it's only caught if the moderation labeler returns `clear_and_obvious_spam`. That's the kind of gap a cheap Jev check on every article would cover.

Want me to apply the fix with a regression spec on a new branch off `main`?

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

---
name: dev-db-mcp-access
description: How to query the DEV/Forem production database directly from Claude Code via the devtodb postgres MCP
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 248ae081-42f9-4561-80cf-a05803a765b5
---

The DEV (dev.to / Forem) production database is queryable from Claude Code via the **`devtodb`** MCP server: `postgres-mcp` pointing at Neon (`ep-silent-lab-…-pooler.us-east-1.aws.neon.tech`, db `forem-primary`), role `readonly_jon_tools`.

Key facts verified 2026-07-13:
- The endpoint we connect to is a **read replica** (`pg_is_in_recovery()` = true) and the role is **read-only server-side** (`transaction_read_only` = on) — despite the branch being named `forem-primary`. Safe to query; writes are impossible.
- Tool: `mcp__devtodb__execute_sql` (plus list_schemas/list_objects/get_object_details/explain_query). Added with `--access-mode=restricted` (redundant given server-side RO, but harmless).
- Config originally lived only in **Claude Desktop** config (`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`), NOT in `~/.claude.json` or the mlh-core/forem project MCP configs. Pulled into Claude Code via `claude mcp add-json devtodb ... -s local`. A newly added MCP server's tools only register on **session restart** (or `/mcp` reconnect).
- Separately, `mlhcoredb` (MLH Core Heroku Postgres, `jon-readonly`) is currently **failing to connect** — different database, not DEV.

This is a live prod replica: prefer single `COUNT`/aggregate queries; avoid scanning `page_views` (huge). Unlike the slopcannon `{database:'dev'}` path (see [[dev-queries]] / [[dev-limitations]] skills), this MCP is a direct psql connection with no ~10s slopcannon budget, but it's still a production replica — be considerate.

content.text:
Two problems stand out in the last 100 AI-checked posts. Spam posts get caught one by one, but the accounts posting them are never suspended. A few spam accounts also get past the checks entirely.

### 1. Nobody gets auto-suspended

Every automatic spam reaction (the "vomit" the mascot account adds) is created with status `valid`. The suspension check only counts reactions with status `confirmed`, i.e. ones a moderator has confirmed. That filter was added deliberately in #22039 (Ben, June 2025) at `app/models/reaction.rb:125`. The result is that bulk spammers never cross the threshold:

| Account | Published posts | Posts in last 24h | Auto spam reactions (30d) | Roles |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `marc_clefas_78e1f2c76e776` | 1,162 | 569 | 1,151 | none |
| `viktoriia_humen_bdaacfa19` | 667 | 157 | 659 | none |
| `rogt7` | 496 | 161 | 2,883 | none |

Each post is caught (score around -210) and still costs us two Gemini calls, and the accounts just keep posting. Your three links are more copies from two of these accounts; the earlier copies were all caught. Fixing this changes a moderation decision someone made on purpose, so it's your call. One option is to count the auto reactions that come with a `clear_and_obvious_spam` label or an `ArticleCheck` YES. Another is a volume rule, such as more than N auto reactions in 24h → give the account the `spam` role.

### 2. Accounts that got through

- **`akbo_ichou_c41c249cc2783d`**: 27 posts in 24h, each a thin "how I built it" post pointing to a different microsite (plantbaes.net, passportcalculator.com, isthisvegan.net, salesemailtemplate.com). `ArticleCheck` said NO on 4 of the 5 I saw. Each post looks fine on its own; the network pattern only shows up across posts, and the check only sees the author's last 10 titles.
- **`vmodal_ai`**: 32 near-identical Kotlin robot tutorials in 24h. The labeler rated most of them `very_good_and_on_topic`, and only 2 got a spam reaction.
- **`rogt7`'s posts without links**: #32 was labeled `likely_spam` (score -66) and #74 `okay_and_on_topic` (score -58), and neither got a reaction. `ArticleCheck` never runs on posts without links. Their negative scores probably keep them out of feeds anyway.

### 3. Spam verdict but no spam reaction (6 posts, cause unknown)

`ArticleCheck` returned YES but no spam reaction exists on these:
- `vmodal_ai`: 4745058, 4745060, 4745070
- `mfc_keibisoft`: 4745071, 4745072 (these look like legitimate product posts, so missing them may be fine)

4744535 (`dimitrios-mikedis`) was labeled `clear_and_obvious_spam` and also has no reaction. Both paths call `Reaction.create`, which fails without raising an error. I found no moderator audit log entries for these posts. The same code works for thousands of other posts, so something specific to these is failing validation or the reaction was deleted afterwards. I didn't dig further.

### Possible false positives
- `beyondmachines` security breach news (#59) got a spam reaction.
- `crawlerbros` NCAA scraping post (#54) got a spam reaction too, though it's arguably promo.

Items 1 and 2 are where a Jev check would pay off: it's cheap enough to run on every post, links or not, and to score account-level signals like "25 near-duplicate posts from one account today". The 21:08 timer for your three original links is still running, and I'll report when it fires.

Hey GnomeMan4201,
Thank you for the report about the three fraud accounts. We have removed their posts and suspended their accounts.

I do see your earlier report as well about additional suspected bot accounts. You had offered to share your methodology for detecting and auditing those accounts - we would be happy to take a look at that if you're open to sharing it.

Gnome Man gnomeman4201@gmail.com via majorleaguehacking.com 
Sat, May 23, 3:47 PM
to DEV, security, abuse

Subject: Re: FOLLOW-UP: Active Fraud Marketplace on DEV.to — 3 accounts, 34 articles, still live

Hey DEV Team,

Thanks for the quick action on those three accounts — glad that got cleaned up.

Happy to share the methodology. I built a small Python audit tool that pulls my follower list via the DEV.to API and scores each account against a set of bot heuristics:

- Auto-generated or hash-style username patterns
- Empty bio
- Zero published articles
- Default profile image
- Disproportionate following/follower ratio (following many, followed by almost no one)
- Account creation date clustering (large numbers of accounts created on the same day)

Each signal adds to a heuristic score. Accounts scoring 3 or above are flagged as likely bots, 1-2 as suspicious. On my account, out of 1,393 followers, 75% had zero posts and no bio, with 497 flagged as likely bots and 896 as suspicious — and 0 scoring as likely real.

The spike went from roughly 600 followers to 1,393 in a matter of days following a post with above-average traction. My GitHub follower count didn't reflect any of this, which is a strong signal it was artificial.

I'm currently finishing a clean re-run of the tool with join date tracking added, which will show account creation clustering. Once that's done I'll send over:

def fetch_followers():
    followers = []
    page = 1
    while True:
        url = f"https://dev.to/api/followers/users?page={page}"
        r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS)
        if r.status_code != 200:
            break
        data = r.json()
        if not data:
            break
        followers.extend(data)
        print(f"📦 Page {page}: +{len(data)} followers")
        page += 1
        time.sleep(1)
    print(f"✅ Total followers fetched: {len(followers)}")
    return followers

def fetch_user_profile(username):
    url = f"https://dev.to/api/users/by_username?url={username}"
    r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS)
    if r.status_code == 200:
        return r.json()
    return {}

def score_account(username):
    if not username:
        return {"Username": None, "HeuristicScore": 0, "HeuristicReasons": "no username"}

    profile = fetch_user_profile(username)
    score = 0
    notes = []

    if re.match(r"^[_\-0-9a-f]{6,}$", username):
        score += 1
        notes.append("Suspicious username")
    if not profile.get("summary"):
        score += 1
        notes.append("Empty bio")
    if profile.get("public_articles_count", 0) == 0:
        score += 1
        notes.append("No posts")
    if profile.get("profile_image", "").endswith("default_profile_image.png"):
        score += 1
        notes.append("Default profile image")

    followers = profile.get("followers_count", 0)
    following = profile.get("followed_users_count", 1)
    if following > 10 and followers / following < 0.1:
        score += 1
        notes.append("Low follower/following ratio")

    joined = profile.get("joined_at", "") or ""
    if joined:
        joined = joined[:10]

    return {
        "Username": username,
        "Bio": profile.get("summary", ""),
        "PostCount": profile.get("public_articles_count", 0),

content.text:
The flagged accounts in the email aren't a botnet. They're ordinary new signups who followed GnomeMan4201 from the onboarding "suggested people to follow" step, and the report's strongest signals come from bugs in their script.

**What prod data shows** (GnomeMan4201 now has 7,562 followers):
- **They followed at signup.** 98% (7,416) followed him within an hour of creating their account, and 99.6% follow more than 10 people. That matches the onboarding step (`Users::SuggestProminent` in `OnboardingsController#suggested_user_follows`), where new users follow a batch of about 19 suggested authors.
- **Signups didn't spike.** DEV signups on May 12–20 were a steady 1,300–2,100 a day. The number of those who followed him swung day to day: 1 → 175 → 217 → 55 → 7 → 313. That looks like his account rotating in and out of the suggestions after his post took off, not a batch of new accounts.
- **The "dormant November accounts" weren't dormant.** They followed him in November 2025, seconds after signing up; for example, `poojitha_katta` signed up at 11:21:27 and followed at 11:22:31. Nothing in the data shows them waking up in May. The accounts they named, like `johnmaveric` and `selvaganesh_js`, look like normal people who signed up and mostly never came back.
- **The "sequential S3 IDs" are just our user IDs.** Upload paths use the user ID, and roughly 9k IDs over 5 days is our normal signup rate.

**Why their script flagged everyone** (`devto_audit_core.py`):
- `profile.get("followed_users_count", 1)`: our `/api/users/by_username` response doesn't include that field, so every account defaults to 1. That's their "every account follows exactly one person: me" finding.
- `profile.get("public_articles_count", 0)`: likely also missing from that response, so every account counts as "no posts". In reality 2,387 of his followers have posts.
- Combined with an empty bio, which is normal for a brand-new account, almost everyone reaches the "bot" score of 2 or more. That's how they got "0 likely real."

There's nothing for spam detection to act on here, and suspending the 899 would hit real users. The earlier report about the three fraud accounts was real, and those accounts were suspended back in May. Their email said they plan to publish a write-up calling this a coordinated botnet, so it's probably worth replying with the onboarding explanation before they do. Want me to draft that reply?

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Gmail__get_thread
entries.description:
Retrieves a specific email thread from the authenticated user's Gmail account, including its `viewUrl` and a list of its messages (each with their own `viewUrl`).

Note: This tool does not support retrieving drafts. Any draft messages within a thread are omitted. To view drafts, use the `list_drafts` tool instead.

The optional `messageFormat` parameter controls the format of the messages returned. By default (or with `FULL_CONTENT`), it returns the full content of messages. We recommend using `PLAIN_TEXT`, which returns the plain text body without the HTML body. Use `MINIMAL` to include only subject and snippet (excluding body). Use `METADATA_ONLY` to include only basic metadata (message ID, thread ID, viewUrl, labels, timestamp, and size estimate).

messageFormat.description: Optional. Specifies the format of the messages returned within the thread. Defaults to `FULL_CONTENT`. We recommend using `PLAIN_TEXT` to prevent context exhaustion. Note: `MINIMAL` format returns `id`, `snippet`, `subject`, `sender`, `to_recipients`, `cc_recipients`, `bcc_recipients`, `date`, `label_ids`. `METADATA_ONLY` format returns `id`, `sender`, `to_recipients`, `cc_recipients`, `bcc_recipients`, `date`, `label_ids`. `FULL_CONTENT` returns `id`, `snippet`, `subject`, `sender`, `to_recipients`, `cc_recipients`, `bcc_recipients`, `date`, `label_ids`, `attachment_ids`, `plaintext_body`, `html_body`, `attachments`. `PLAIN_TEXT` returns `id`, `snippet`, `subject`, `sender`, `to_recipients`, `cc_recipients`, `bcc_recipients`, `date`, `label_ids`, `attachment_ids`, `plaintext_body`, `attachments` (without `html_body`). `RAW` format is not supported here.
x-google-enum-descriptions: Returns all message fields (`id`, `snippet`, `subject`, `sender`, `to_recipients`, `cc_recipients`, `bcc_recipients`, `date`, `label_ids`, `attachment_ids`, `plaintext_body`, `html_body`, `attachments`, `view_url`) if applicable.

Returns all information in `MINIMAL` plus `plaintext_body`, `attachment_ids`, and `attachments` (if applicable). If plain text body is not available, converts the HTML body to plain text/markdown. Omits `html_body`.
Returns the raw MIME message content.

threadId.description: Required. The unique identifier of the thread to fetch.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Gmail__search_threads
entries.description:
Lists email threads from the authenticated user's Gmail account.

This tool can filter threads based on a query string and supports pagination. It returns a list of threads, including their IDs, `viewUrl`, and related messages (each with their own `viewUrl`). Each related message contains details like a snippet of the message body, the subject, the sender, the recipients etc. The `view` parameter controls which fields are populated in the related messages. By default (or with `THREAD_VIEW_MINIMAL`), it includes subject and snippet. Use `THREAD_VIEW_METADATA_ONLY` to exclude subject and snippet. Note that the full message bodies are not returned by this tool; use the 'get_thread' tool with a thread ID to fetch the full message body if needed. Threads with excluded criteria may still appear in the results. This occurs because Gmail identifies matching messages first. For example, if you search for -is:starred, Gmail will find an entire thread if it contains at least one unstarred message, even if other emails in that same conversation are starred.

Note: An empty JSON object `{}` represents zero matching items, not an error.

includeTrash.description: Optional. Include threads from TRASH in the results. Defaults to false.

pageSize.description: Optional. The maximum number of threads to return. If unspecified, defaults to 20. The maximum allowed value is 50.

pageToken.description: Optional. Page token to retrieve a specific page of results in the list. Leave empty to fetch the first page. This is primarily used for pagination to continue fetching results from where the previous `SearchThreads` call left off, especially when the number of threads matching the query exceeds the `page_size` limit.

query.description: Optional. A query string to filter the threads. Natural language queries must be pre-converted into Gmail syntax queries to use this tool. If omitted, all threads (excluding spam and trash by default) are listed. Supported Operators by Category: Sender & Recipient: - `from:` — Sent from a specific person. - `to:` — Sent to a specific person. - `cc:` — Specific people in Cc. - `bcc:` — Specific people in Bcc. - `deliveredto:` — Delivered to a specific address. - `list:` — From a specific mailing list. Time & Date: - `after:YYYY/MM/DD` / `newer:YYYY/MM/DD` — Received after a date. - `before:YYYY/MM/DD` / `older:YYYY/MM/DD` — Received before a date. - `older_than:` — Older than a duration (for example, `1y`, `2d`). - `newer_than:` — Newer than a duration. Content: - `subject:` — Words in the subject line. - `has:` — Has specific content types (attachment, drive, youtube, document). - `filename:` — Attachment with a specific name or type. - `""` — Search for an exact word or phrase. (for example, `"holiday"`, `"holiday vacation"`). Note: Double quotes enforce strict contiguous phrase matching. For topic, discussion, or keyword queries, prefer unquoted keywords (e.g. `partner advertising` instead of `"partner advertising"`). - `+` — Match a word exactly. (for example, `+holiday`, `+unicorn`) - `rfc822msgid:` — Specific message ID header. - `AROUND ` — Find words near each other (for example, `holiday AROUND 10 vacation`). Labels & Categories: - `label:` — Under a specific label. The tool accepts label IDs, not display names. Use the `list_labels` tool to get the ID. - `category:` — In a category (primary, social, promotions, updates, forums, reservations, purchases). - `in:` — Search in specific labels (archive, snoozed, trash, sent, inbox). For example, `in:trash`, `in:inbox`. Archived and sent messages are included by default; use `-in:archive` and `-in:sent` to exclude them. Drafts are explicitly excluded by default by the tool. Use `in:inbox` to restrict search to the inbox only. - `has:userlabels` — Has any user labels. - `has:nouserlabels` — Does not have any user labels. - `has:*-star` — Specific star colors (if enabled, for example, `has:yellow-star`). - `in:draft` — Search in drafts. -in:draft means exclude drafts from the search results. - `in:sent` — Search in sent messages. - `in:anywhere` — Search in all folders (including spam and trash). Status: - `is:` — Search by status (important, starred, unread, read, muted). Size: - `size:` — Specific size in bytes. - `larger:` / `smaller:` — Larger or smaller than a size (for example, `10M` for 10 MB). Logic & Grouping: - `AND` — Match all criteria (default behavior). - `OR` or `{ }` — Match one or more criteria (for example, `from:amy OR from:david`, `{from:amy from:david}`). - `-` (minus) — Exclude criteria (for example, `-movie`). - `( )` — Group multiple search terms (for example, `subject:(dinner film)`). Examples: - `subject:OneMCP Update` - `from:user@example.com` - `to:user2@example.com AND newer_than:7d` - `project proposal has:attachment` - `is:unread -in:draft` To prevent overly strict queries, favor concise, keyword-based queries over long subject strings or full sentences. Avoid copying overly detailed subjects from the user prompt verbatim, as this often leads to search misses. Instead, extract the most unique keywords (e.g., subject:amazon \"delivery\" OR \"order\" instead of \"amazon order\"). Use boolean operators to broaden your search coverage. Use OR to search for synonyms or multiple potential senders, and use ( ) for grouping criteria. Note that whitespace between terms acts as an implicit AND.

view.description: Optional. Controls the fields populated for threads in the thread list. Defaults to `THREAD_VIEW_MINIMAL`. `THREAD_VIEW_MINIMAL` returns `id`, `snippet`, `subject`, `sender`, `to_recipients`, `cc_recipients`, `bcc_recipients`, `date`, `label_ids`. `THREAD_VIEW_METADATA_ONLY` returns `id`, `sender`, `to_recipients`, `cc_recipients`, `bcc_recipients`, `date`, `label_ids`.

lastPrompt: help me look at his fraud accounts, and the spam content we found ourselves - what can we do to improve spam flags and repeat offender detection

aiTitle: Spam detection with jev and gemini

content.text:
Your three original links were all caught at 21:05:20 UTC by the cleanup job, 26–29 minutes after they were published. Each got the `clear_and_obvious_spam` label and a spam reaction, including the car-fridge post, so the delay I found earlier is confirmed.

## GnomeMan4201's fraud accounts (reported May 22)

| Account | Posts | Auto-flagged by our checks | Still published |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rraghucrchikkade` (verified Stripe/Binance accounts, fake reviews) | 32 | 31 | 32 |
| `make_olise_04687327efa4a8` (counterfeit euros, fake language certificates, Caluanie) | 7 | 6 | 7 |
| `us_eu_service` (KYC-verified bank and exchange accounts) | 10 | 5 | 10 |

- **Our detection caught most of these posts, but nothing escalated.** All 42 flagged posts got a spam reaction, yet none of the accounts were suspended until a human acted on the email. `rraghucrchikkade` kept posting for about 40 hours after the first flags.
- **`us_eu_service` was half missed** because its posts had Telegram and Discord handles written as plain text, not links, so `ArticleCheck` never ran on them.
- **All 49 posts are still live today.** The accounts were suspended by hand, but suspending doesn't unpublish anything, so our reply saying "we have removed their posts" wasn't accurate. The counterfeit-currency page returns HTTP 200 with the WhatsApp and Telegram contacts showing (it's `noindex`, so it's not in Google). These should be unpublished now regardless of anything else in this list.

## What to change, in order of impact

1. **Automatically act on repeat offenders.** The suspension check only counts moderator-`confirmed` reactions (#22039), and the automatic ones are `valid`, so it never fires. In the last 2 days, **813 accounts got 3 or more automatic spam flags (8,181 flags total) and 2 were actioned**; 64 of them had 20 or more. I sampled 20 accounts at the lowest tier (3–5 flags): about 15 were plain spam (loans, garage doors, piracy, "net worth", SEO accounts) and the rest were low-value self-promo or content farms. None looked like a real developer. Suggested rule: count an automatic flag only when it has a clear-spam label or an `ArticleCheck` YES, and only for low-trust accounts (few badges, recently joined). At the threshold, give the account the `spam` role rather than suspending it.
2. **Unpublish or hide posts when an account gets the `spam` or `suspended` role.** Today only automatic suspension unpublishes, and only when the `unpublish_all_posts_when_user_auto_suspended` flag is on, so manual actions leave everything live.
3. **Cap daily posting for low-trust accounts.** The only limits are 1 post per 30 seconds, or 1 per 5 minutes for accounts under 3 days old, and there's no daily cap. `marc_clefas` posted 569 articles today and `rraghucrchikkade` 29 in one day. Something like 5 a day for accounts with 0 badges would have stopped every bulk account in this session.
4. **Use the article embeddings we already generate to catch duplicates.** `GenerateArticleEmbeddingWorker` already stores an embedding for every post. Comparing a new post against the author's last 20 would flag the reposted massage and spreadsheet posts and the `vmodal_ai` templates without an extra LLM call.
5. **Check spam in posts without links.** Add contact patterns (Telegram, WhatsApp, phone numbers) as triggers, or run a cheap classifier such as Jev on every post from low-trust accounts. This covers `us_eu_service` and `rogt7`'s posts without links.
6. **Fix the transaction-commit race** with the `after_all_transactions_commit` change from earlier. Right now most new spam sits unlabeled for 10–40 minutes.
7. **Stop discarding failed spam reactions.** `Reaction.create` fails without raising or logging. Six posts in today's sample were judged spam but have no reaction.

Items 1 and 3 would also cut Gemini spend, since every repost from a known spammer costs two Gemini calls.

Item 1 reverses Ben's deliberate choice, so it's worth checking with him before changing it. Items 2, 3 and 6 are small, separate PRs I can start on a branch off `main`. For the fraud posts, I only have read-only DB access, so unpublishing needs someone with admin or console access.

name: forem-local-dev-env-gotchas
description: Two silent Forem local-dev traps — pg/libpq GSS segfault in forked Puma workers on macOS, and strong_migrations 1.8 making rails db:migrate a no-op on Rails 8
metadata:
  type: project
---

Local Forem dev (macOS, Aug 2026) has two failures that look like config loss but are not:

1. **Puma workers segfault on every DB request.** The precompiled `pg-1.6.3-arm64-darwin` gem bundles libpq 18, whose `PQconnectStart` → `pg_GSS_have_cred_cache` → Kerberos/Heimdal → CoreFoundation call is not fork-safe. With `preload_app!` + `WEB_CONCURRENCY=2` in `config/puma.rb`, every forked worker dies with SIGSEGV. Fix: `PGGSSENCMODE=disable` in `.env` (added 2026-08-27). Non-forked `PG.connect` works fine, which is why it only shows up under the server.

2. **`rails db:migrate` silently runs nothing** and just prints "Dumping schema". `strong_migrations` is pinned `~> 1.7` in the Gemfile → resolves to 1.8.0, whose `DatabaseTasks#migrate(*args)` override drops keyword args; Rails 8's `migrate_all` calls `migrate(skip_initialize: true)`, so that hash lands in the `version` slot and the filter block matches no migration. Upstream fixed it in strong_migrations 2.0.2 ("Fixed migrations not running with Active Record 8"). Until the Gemfile is bumped to `~> 2.0`, migrate one at a time with `rails db:migrate:up VERSION=...`.

3. **Schema dumps drop unrelated columns/indexes.** Because of (2), the local DB is usually behind on recent migrations, so `db:migrate:up` re-dumps `schema.rb` without them (seen 2026-09-04: lost `favorited_weight`, `index_articles_on_published_at_and_score`, a recommended_articles_lists index). After any migration: `git checkout db/schema.rb`, then hand-add only the version bump and your own change, per AGENTS.md.

Also: ruby is pinned 3.4.9 by `~/Documents/GitHub/mise.toml`, which overrides Forem's `.ruby-version` (3.3.0); `forem/.mise.toml` now sets `ruby = "3.3.0"`. Forem runs on port 3006 behind Caddy (`forem.mlh.test`), see [[forem-fork-hygiene]].

module Moderator
  class ManageActivityAndRoles
    attr_reader :user, :admin, :user_params

    def self.handle_user_roles(admin:, user:, user_params:)
      new(user: user, admin: admin, user_params: user_params).update_roles
    end

    def initialize(user:, admin:, user_params:)
      @user = user
      @admin = admin
      @user_params = user_params
    end

    def delete_comments
      Users::DeleteComments.call(user)
    end

    def delete_articles
      Users::DeleteArticles.call(user)
    end

    def delete_user_activity
      Users::DeleteActivity.call(user)
    end

    def delete_user_podcasts
      Users::DeletePodcasts.call(user)
    end

    def remove_privileges
      remove_mod_roles
      remove_tag_moderator_role
    end

    def remove_notifications
      Notifications::RemoveBySpammerWorker.perform_async(user.id)
    end

    def remove_mod_roles
      Tag.with_role(:tag_moderator, @user).find_each(&:touch)
      @user.remove_role(:trusted)
      @user.remove_role(:tag_moderator)
      @user.notification_setting.update(email_tag_mod_newsletter: false)
      Mailchimp::Bot.new(user).manage_tag_moderator_list
      @user.notification_setting.update(email_community_mod_newsletter: false)
      Mailchimp::Bot.new(user).manage_community_moderator_list
    end

    def remove_tag_moderator_role
      Tag.with_role(:tag_moderator, @user).find_each(&:touch)
      @user.remove_role(:tag_moderator)
      Mailchimp::Bot.new(user).manage_tag_moderator_list
    end

    def create_note(reason, content)
      Note.create(
        author_id: @admin.id,
        noteable_id: @user.id,
        noteable_type: "User",
        reason: reason,
        content: content || "#{@admin.username} updated #{@user.username}",
      )
    end

    # rubocop:disable Metrics/CyclomaticComplexity
    def handle_user_status(role, note)
      case role
      when "Admin"
        assign_elevated_role_to_user(user, :admin)
        TagModerators::AddTrustedRole.call(user)
      when "Comment Suspended"
        comment_suspended
      when "Limited"
        limited
      when "Suspended" || "Spammer"
        user.add_role(:suspended)
        remove_privileges
      when "Spam"
        user.add_role(:spam)
        remove_privileges
        remove_notifications
        resolve_spam_reports
        confirm_flag_reactions
        user.profile.touch
      when "Super Moderator"
        assign_elevated_role_to_user(user, :super_moderator)
        TagModerators::AddTrustedRole.call(user)
      when "Good standing"
        regular_member
      when /^(Resource Admin: )/
        check_super_admin
        remove_negative_roles
        user.add_role(:single_resource_admin, role.split("Resource Admin: ").last.safe_constantize)
      when "Super Admin"
        assign_elevated_role_to_user(user, :super_admin)
        TagModerators::AddTrustedRole.call(user)
      when "Tech Admin"
        assign_elevated_role_to_user(user, :tech_admin)
        # DataUpdateScripts falls under the admin namespace
        # and hence requires a single_resource_admin role to view
        # this technical admin resource
        user.add_role(:single_resource_admin, DataUpdateScript)
      when "Trusted"
        remove_negative_roles
        TagModerators::AddTrustedRole.call(user)
      when "Community Leader Level 1"
        assign_community_leader_role(:community_leader_level_1)
      when "Community Leader Level 2"
        assign_community_leader_role(:community_leader_level_2)
      when "Warned"
        warned
      when "Base Subscriber"
        base_subscriber
      end
      create_note(role, note)

      user.articles.published.find_each(&:async_score_calc)
      user.comments.find_each(&:calculate_score)
    end
    # rubocop:enable Metrics/CyclomaticComplexity

    def assign_elevated_role_to_user(user, role)
      check_super_admin
      remove_negative_roles
      user.add_role(role)

      # Clear cache key if the elevated role matches Rack::Attack bypass roles
      return unless Rack::Attack::ADMIN_ROLES.include?(role.to_s)

      Rails.cache.delete(Rack::Attack::ADMIN_API_CACHE_KEY)
    end

    def check_super_admin
      raise I18n.t("services.moderator.manage_activity_and_roles.need_super") unless @admin.super_admin?
    end

    def assign_community_leader_role(role)
      remove_negative_roles
      CommunityLeaders::Add.call(user, role)
module Moderator
  class UnpublishAllArticlesWorker
    include Sidekiq::Job

    ALLOWED_LISTENERS = %i[admin_api moderator].freeze
    DEFAULT_LISTENER = :admin_api

    sidekiq_options queue: :medium_priority, retry: 10

    # @param target_user_id [Integer] the user who is being unpublished
    # @param action_user_id [Integer] the user who takes action / unpublishes
    def perform(target_user_id, action_user_id, listener = "admin_api")
      listener = listener.to_sym
      listener = DEFAULT_LISTENER unless ALLOWED_LISTENERS.include?(listener)
      UnpublishAllArticles.call(target_user_id: target_user_id,
                                action_user_id: action_user_id,
                                listener: listener.to_sym)
    end
  end
end

        confirm_flag_reactions
        user.profile.touch
      when "Super Moderator"
        assign_elevated_role_to_user(user, :super_moderator)
        TagModerators::AddTrustedRole.call(user)
      when "Good standing"
        regular_member
      when /^(Resource Admin: )/

        remove_negative_roles
        user.add_role(:single_resource_admin, role.split("Resource Admin: ").last.safe_constantize)

content.content:
# jev-1.13 Strengths and Weaknesses

**Strengths:**
- Excels at "System One" tasks requiring common-sense judgment
- Fast and well-calibrated for its intended use case
- Highly consistent across semantically similar inputs

**Key Weaknesses:**

*Task Limitations:*
- Struggles with "tasks that require additional levels of indirection" and multi-hop reasoning
- Poor at numeric precision and mathematical calculations
- Unreliable for counting items or tallying occurrences
- Cannot reliably compare dates or perform temporal arithmetic
- "Not trained to generate text"

*Input Sensitivity:*
- Literal interpretation of instructions; misses implied intent
- Performance degrades significantly with "large state full of irrelevant detail"
- Context rot: unrelated information in state reduces accuracy
- Bounded context window (see Models page for limits)

*Robustness Issues:*
- Vulnerable to adversarial content: "injected instruction, deliberately misleading framing, or text that argues for its own classification, can move the answer"
- Not designed to treat state as "hostile by default"
- Susceptible to prompt injection and steered responses

*Calibration Caveats:*
- Score outputs lack "numerical calibration" for precise magnitude reconstruction
- Structural invariants not guaranteed (e.g., P(noul) ≠ 1 - P(not noul))
- Choice and Noul outputs are not directly interchangeable

**Recommendation:** Avoid math, generation, adversarial scenarios, and complex indirection. Offload computations to code.

content.content:
# TypeSafe's Probabilities and Confidence System

## How Probabilities Work

TypeSafe returns a `probabilities` property representing the distribution across options (for Choice questions) or levels (for Score assessments). The *shape* of this distribution reveals certainty: concentrated probability indicates confidence, while spread-out distributions signal uncertainty.

## Confidence Calculation

Confidence is a derived statistic that collapses the probability distribution into a single 0-1 number. As the documentation explains: "All of it on one option gives 1.0; the more evenly it spreads, the lower the confidence." The system computes this automatically for Choice and Score answers, eliminating manual calculations.

## Calibration & Measurement

Rather than traditional probability calibration, TypeSafe measures certainty through distribution shape. Low confidence on a Choice typically means no clear winner among options; on a Score, it suggests ambiguous levels or insufficient state information.

Importantly: "If an intelligent system cannot express honest uncertainty, the system cannot be trusted." Confidence functions as a built-in mechanism for models to communicate doubt.

## Recommended Thresholding Patterns

TypeSafe suggests dividing confidence into three ranges:

- **High confidence (typically >0.9):** Act automatically without human involvement
- **Medium confidence:** "Proceed with caution...you might ask the user to confirm, flag for review, or gather more information"
- **Low confidence (<0.5):** Route to humans, request clarification, or use alternative systems

The key principle: "A confidence threshold is not one number. Different actions within the same system should be gated at different levels depending on the consequences of getting it wrong."

The documentation emphasizes testing with your own data and adjusting thresholds based on domain-specific risk tolerance and observed model performance.

# Benchmark Summary: Jev vs Trained Spam Classifiers

## Datasets
Two public corpora evaluated on fixed stratified holdouts:
- **SMS Spam Collection**: 5,574 messages (13.4% spam)
- **Enron-Spam**: 4,800 train / 1,000 test (~50% spam)

## Performance Comparison

**SMS Holdout (F1 scores):**
- Jev (zero-shot): 0.952
- Naive Bayes (full 4,574 labels): 0.973
- LinearSVC (calibrated): lags behind Jev
- Claude Haiku 4.5: 0.851

**Enron Holdout:**
- Jev: 0.955
- Naive Bayes: 0.984
- Claude Haiku: 0.980

Jev requires approximately 2,000 labeled examples' worth of performance to match trained models in-domain.

## Cross-Domain Collapse
When training on one corpus and testing the other, trained classifiers catastrophically fail:
- ROC-AUC drops from ~0.99 to 0.58–0.64 (near random chance)
- LinearSVC trained on SMS achieves 31.2% accuracy on Enron—worse than always predicting ham
- Jev's single domain-neutral prompt maintains 0.9986 (SMS) and 0.9926 (Enron) ROC-AUC

## Cost & Speed
Against Claude Haiku 4.5 per 1,000 SMS messages:
- **Cost**: Jev $0.0154 vs Haiku $0.3612 (24× cheaper)
- **Latency**: Jev 280ms vs Haiku 780ms median (2.8× faster)

Jev returned 64 distinct probability values; Haiku returned only 16.

## Imbalance Resilience
At severe imbalance (0.2% spam), Jev's false-positive rate "holds at 1.19–1.23%" across severity levels. Threshold retuning restores F1 to 0.902 (95% recovery). Trained classifiers collapse irreparably.

## Key Caveat
In-domain with full training data, Naive Bayes still outperforms Jev marginally (0.973 vs 0.937 on SMS). The trade accepts modest F1 loss for robustness beyond the training domain.

content.text:
#1, #6 and #7 are done on branch `spam-repeat-offender-fixes` (off `main`, not committed). The spam handler and article specs pass (59 examples, 0 failures), and RuboCop reports nothing new apart from one nesting warning that the neighbouring tests already have.

## What changed

- **#1: repeat offenders** (`app/services/spam/handler.rb`). A low-trust author (fewer than 4 badges) now gets the `spam` role when they have 3 or more automatic spam reactions in the last 30 days on published posts labeled `clear_and_obvious_*`. Moderator-confirmed reactions still lead to suspension exactly as before. This follows `handle_profile_update!`, which already adds the `spam` role for clear profile spam.
  - Against the last 2 days of prod data, the rule would have marked 693 accounts.
  - I spot-checked 20 at exactly 3 flags: 19 were plainly commercial spam (dentists, DeFi tokens, snacks, physician mailing lists). One (`revenue_search_…`, content marketing) is arguable.
  - Nothing is backfilled. Accounts get marked on their next clear-spam post, which for the bulk spammers means within minutes of deploy.
- **#6: commit race** (`app/models/article.rb`). The spam worker is now queued with `ActiveRecord.after_all_transactions_commit`, so it runs only after the article is saved and published.
- **#7: failed spam reactions.** Failures are now logged, except the expected "this reaction already exists" case. The root cause turned out to be #6: all six posts were drafts that had just been published, and the reaction was rejected because the worker still saw them as unpublished.
- **Tests:** two regression specs in `spec/services/spam/handler_spec.rb`. The low-trust author gets the `spam` role, and an author with 4 badges doesn't. Drop them if you'd rather not keep them.
- **#2** needs no code, as agreed. One manual step: the three fraud accounts should be switched from "Suspended" to "Spam" in admin, which hides their 49 posts.

## Jev for #5

Jev removes the rule that the Gemini `ArticleCheck` only runs on posts containing a link. A Jev call on a ~1k-token excerpt costs about $0.00004, so every post from a low-trust author can be checked, with or without links.

- **One call, several questions**, each answered as a probability:
  - Is this post spam (promotion or solicitation rather than a real contribution)?
  - Does it ask readers to get in touch off-platform (Telegram, WhatsApp, phone)?
  - Which category is it: dev content, self-promotion, SEO/affiliate, illegal goods, scam, or gibberish?
- **Three ways to act on the answer:**
  - Above ~0.95: add the spam reaction directly, as the clear label does today.
  - Middle: send to the Gemini `ArticleCheck` we already have.
  - Below ~0.3: skip it.

  We'd pick the real thresholds after running Jev in shadow mode (logging only) against the reactions moderators confirm.
- **What it would have caught:** `us_eu_service` (Telegram handles, no links), `rogt7`'s posts without links, and probably the `akbo_ichou` microsite network through the self-promotion category.
- **Where it's weak** (from TypeSafe's own docs): it isn't built to treat input as hostile. Text that argues for its own classification ("this is a legitimate tutorial…") can shift the answer. It also gets less accurate with long, irrelevant input, and it can't count, so "25 posts today" has to be computed in code.
- **What that means for the design:** Jev decides which posts get the Gemini check; code signals stay in place. A contact-pattern regex can't be talked out of its answer, so it should still force a check whenever it matches.
- **Cost and speed:** about $1 a day at our volume, roughly 300–600ms per call inside the worker. In a public benchmark it roughly matched a spam classifier trained on ~2,000 labelled examples, with no training data of its own. It also held up when tested on a different kind of spam, where the trained classifiers dropped to near chance.

My recommendation is to add the regex contact-pattern check to this branch now and do Jev as the next PR, in shadow mode first. Do you want that, and do we have a TypeSafe API key?

Better Stack: request context on unhandled exceptions, Fastly client IP
---
## What

This is a follow-up to #23881, fixing two problems found on DEV.to after deploy.

1. **Unhandled exceptions had no request context.** `logtail-rack`'s `HTTPContext` is added with `config.app_middleware.use`, which puts it below `ActionDispatch::DebugExceptions`. Its context is set in a `CurrentContext.with { }` block that clears it when the exception passes back up. So by the time `DebugExceptions` logs the trace, host, path, method and request_id are gone. On prod, `QueryCanceled` traces arrived with no `context.http`.
2. **`remote_addr` was Fastly's edge IP** (e.g. `167.82.161.32`),
=====
Better Stack: use logtail-rails for request context, keep stdout unchanged, cut noise
---
## What

This switches Better Stack logging from plain `logtail` to `logtail-rails`, so Better Stack lines get request context. It also cuts the noise we've been seeing in the DEV.to source. stdout, and so Datadog, stays the same.

It still only runs in production with `BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN` set. The gem is `require: false` and is only required in `config/application.rb` when that token is set, so other Forem installs never load it.

## What Better Stack gets now
- `context.http` on every line inside a request: host, method, path, client IP, request_id
- `context.user` with the user's **id

Ship production logs to Better Stack (env-gated)
---
## What

When `BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN` is set, production Rails logs go to Better Stack as well as to the existing logger (stdout on Heroku). When it isn't set, nothing changes: the gem is `require: false` and isn't loaded.

- `Gemfile`: add `logtail` (Better Stack's plain Ruby gem), `require: false`, pinned to `~> 0.1.17`
- `config/initializers/betterstack.rb`: adds a `Logtail::Logger` to `Rails.logger` with `broadcast_to`, at the Rails log level. It adds to whatever logger Rails built (stdout, or the default file logger when `RAILS_LOG_TO_STDOUT` isn't set) rather than replacing it.
